t1.text: All of this, a thousandfold and colourful, had always been there, the sun and the moon had always shone, always rivers had roared and bees had buzzed, but in former times all of this had been nothing more to Siddhartha than a fleeting, deceptive veil before his eyes, looked upon in distrust, destined to be penetrated and destroyed by thought, since it was not the essential existence, since this essence lay beyond, on the other side of, the visible. But now, his liberated eyes stayed on this side, he saw and became aware of the visible, sought to be at home in this world, did not search for the true essence, did not aim at a world beyond.

t2.text: "Yes," said the ferryman, "a very beautiful river, I love it more than anything. Often I have listened to it, often I have looked into its eyes, and always I have learned from it. Much can be learned from a river." "I thank you, my benefactor," spoke Siddhartha, disembarking on the other side of the river. "I have no gift I could give you for your hospitality, my dear, and also no payment for your work. I am a man without a home, a son of a Brahmin and a Samana." "I did see it," spoke the ferryman, "and I haven't expected any payment from you and no gift which would be the custom for guests to bear. You will give me the gift another time."

t3.text: "Surely. This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back! You too, Samana, will come back. Now farewell! Let your friendship be my reward. Commemorate me when you make offerings to the gods." Smiling, they parted. Smiling, Siddhartha was happy about the friendship and the kindness of the ferryman. "He is like Govinda," he thought with a smile, "all I meet on my path are like Govinda. All are thankful, though they are the ones who would have a right to receive thanks. All are submissive, all would like to be friends, like to obey, think little. Like children are all people."

t4.text: Thus I am entering this city, Siddhartha thought, with a charming omen. He instantly felt drawn into the grove, but he thought about it, and only now he became aware of how the servants and maids had looked at him at the entrance, how despicable, how distrustful, how rejecting. I am still a Samana, he thought, I am still an ascetic and beggar. I must not remain like this, I will not be able to enter the grove like this. And he laughed.

t5.text: "Never before has this happened to me, my friend, that a Samana from the forest came to me and wanted to learn from me! Never before has this happened to me, that a Samana comes to me with long hair and an old, torn loincloth! Many young men come to me, and there are also sons of Brahmins among them, but they come in beautiful clothes, they come in fine shoes, they have perfume in their hair and money in their pouches. This is, O Samana, what the young men are like who come to me."

t6.text: Did any Samana or Brahmin ever fear that someone might come and grab him and steal his learning, and his religious devotion, and his depth of thought? No, for they are his very own, and he would only give away from those whatever he is willing to give and to whomever he is willing to give. Like this it is, precisely like this it is also with Kamala and with the pleasures of love. Beautiful and red is Kamala's mouth, but just try to kiss it against Kamala's will, and you will not obtain a single drop of sweetness from it, which knows how to give so many sweet things! You are learning easily, Siddhartha, thus you should also learn this: love can be obtained by begging, buying, receiving it as a gift, finding it in the street, but it cannot be stolen.

t7.text: "Friend, many would like to know this. You must do what you've learned and ask for money, clothes, and shoes in return. There is no other way for a poor man to obtain money. What might you be able to do?" "I can think. I can wait. I can fast."

t8.text: "Simple is the life which people lead in this world here," thought Siddhartha. "It presents no difficulties. Everything was difficult, toilsome, and ultimately hopeless, when I was still a Samana. Now, everything is easy, easy like that lessons in kissing, which Kamala is giving me. I need clothes and money, nothing else; this a small, near goals, they won't make a person lose any sleep."

t9.text: When you throw a rock into the water, it will speed on the fastest course to the bottom of the water. This is how it is when Siddhartha has a goal, a resolution. Siddhartha does nothing, he waits, he thinks, he fasts, but he passes through the things of the world like a rock through water, without doing anything, without stirring; he is drawn, he lets himself fall. His goal attracts him, because he doesn't let anything enter his soul which might oppose the goal. This is what Siddhartha has learned among the Samanas. This is what fools call magic and of which they think it would be effected by means of the daemons. Nothing is effected by daemons, there are no daemons. Everyone can perform magic, everyone can reach his goals, if he is able to think, if he is able to wait, if he is able to fast."

t10.text: Pursuing his goal, he allowed the city to suck him in, drifted through the flow of the streets, stood still on the squares, rested on the stairs of stone by the river. When the evening came, he made friends with barber's assistant, whom he had seen working in the shade of an arch in a building, whom he found again praying in a temple of Vishnu, whom he told about stories of Vishnu and the Lakshmi. Among the boats by the river, he slept this night, and early in the morning, before the first customers came into his shop, he had the barber's assistant shave his beard and cut his hair, comb his hair and anoint it with fine oil. Then he went to take his bath in the river.

t11.text: Contently, he did as he had been told. Being accustomed to the forest, he managed to get out of the grove and over the hedge without making a sound. Contently, he returned to the city, carrying the rolled up garments under his arm. At the inn, where travellers stay, he positioned himself by the door, without words he asked for food, without a word he accepted a piece of rice cake. Perhaps as soon as tomorrow, he thought, I will ask no one for food any more. Suddenly, pride flared up in him. He was no Samana any more, it was no longer becoming to him to beg. He gave the rice cake to a dog and remained without food.

t13.text: But to the maid she gave the order to give the pious Brahmin white upper garments. Without fully understanding what was happening to him, Siddhartha found himself being dragged away by the maid, brought into a garden-house avoiding the direct path, being given upper garments as a gift, led into the bushes, and urgently admonished to get himself out of the grove as soon as possible without being seen.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha discovers that the sun and moon have only now begun to shine.
Siddhartha longs to return to the forest of the Samanas.
Siddhartha decides that the visible world is a deceptive veil that he must destroy by careful thought.
Siddhartha now accepts the visible world instead of trying to see past it.
A.explanation: Before, the world was "a fleeting, deceptive veil" to be "penetrated"; "now, his liberated eyes stayed on this side." Destroying a "deceptive veil" by thought is his old view. The sun and moon "had always shone." No wish to return to the Samanas appears.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what does the ferryman say about payment?
options: He demands a fair payment and grows angry when none is given.
He asks Siddhartha to stay and help him work on the raft for a while.
He expected none and says Siddhartha will give a gift another time.
He wants a poem or a song in return.
A.explanation: The ferryman says, "I haven't expected any payment" and "You will give me the gift another time." He is not angry and makes no demand. Work on the raft is not requested. A poem is what Kamala later asks for, not the ferryman.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "anoint" most nearly means
options: rub with oil
bless with a prayer
cut short
wash with river water
A.explanation: The assistant should "anoint it with fine oil," so it means rub with oil. Cutting is a separate step ("cut his hair"). Washing comes later, in the river bath. "Bless with a prayer" is a religious sense of anoint, but here the oil is for grooming.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha realizes he
options: is admired by all of Kamala's servants
should give up and return to the forest
must change how he looks before he can enter the grove
is already welcome there and should walk straight in to greet her
A.explanation: Noticing the servants' scornful looks, he thinks, "I must not remain like this, I will not be able to enter the grove like this." He is not welcome yet. He laughs rather than gives up. The servants looked at him with distrust, not admiration.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Kamala say a poor man must do to obtain money?
options: Borrow it from a merchant in the city.
Do what he has learned and ask for payment.
Wait patiently for it to come to him.
Beg at the doors of rich houses, as Samanas do.
A.explanation: Kamala says, "You must do what you've learned and ask for money, clothes, and shoes in return. There is no other way." Begging is not her advice; she says there is no other way. Borrowing is not mentioned. Waiting is one of Siddhartha's skills, not her rule.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "You must do what you've learned and ask for money, clothes, and shoes"
"Friend, many would like to know this."
"What might you be able to do?"
"I can think. I can wait. I can fast."
A.explanation: Only "You must do what you've learned and ask for money" states her rule. "Many would like to know this" only notes the question is common. "What might you be able to do?" asks about his skills. "I can think..." is Siddhartha's answer, not her rule.

A.prompt: The repeated phrase "Never before has this happened to me" mainly serves to
options: introduce Kamala's many servants and maids
stress how unusual Siddhartha's request is to Kamala
show that Kamala is frightened and wants him gone
show that Kamala is bored by his visit
A.explanation: Kamala repeats it while laughing, stressing how unusual it is for a Samana to come to learn from her. She is amused, not frightened. Boredom does not fit her laughter. The servants are not mentioned in this passage, which is all Kamala's own speech.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha decides to return the fine garments he was given.
Siddhartha is caught sneaking out of Kamala's grove.
Siddhartha begs for food at the inn and eats with the other travellers.
Proud that he is no longer a Samana, Siddhartha refuses to beg.
A.explanation: "Pride flared up in him. He was no Samana any more, it was no longer becoming to him to beg," so he gives the cake to a dog. He does not eat it. He leaves "without making a sound," uncaught. He carries the garments away; returning them is not mentioned.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what has the ferryman learned from the river?
options: That the river must never be crossed at night
That gifts must be paid back at once
That everything comes back
That Samanas never come back
A.explanation: He says, "This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back!" Danger is not mentioned. He says "You too, Samana, will come back," the opposite of Samanas never returning. He says the gift can come at some later time.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "despicable" most nearly means
options: hidden
scornful
tired
admiring
A.explanation: The servants looked at him "how despicable, how distrustful, how rejecting," so their looks were scornful. Admiring looks contradict "rejecting." "Tired" and "hidden" do not describe how one looks at a stranger with rejection, so they cannot fit this sentence.

options: must be given freely to be had at all
can be taken by any man strong and bold enough
is worth far less than learning
belongs only to the Samanas
A.explanation: Kissing her "against Kamala's will" brings "not... a single drop of sweetness," and love "cannot be stolen," so it must be given freely. That denies taking it by strength. She compares love to learning rather than ranking it below. Samanas are compared, not given sole claim.

A.prompt: The comparison "like a rock through water" suggests that Siddhartha moves toward his goals
options: noisily, with great splashing
slowly and afraid of sinking
by pushing others aside
steadily and without struggle
A.explanation: A thrown rock goes "on the fastest course to the bottom," and he passes through "without doing anything, without stirring," so the image is steady movement without struggle. A rock does not hesitate or fear. "Without stirring" rules out noise. Nothing suggests pushing others aside.

B.prompt: According to Kamala, in which way can love NOT be obtained?
options: By buying it with money
By finding it in the street
By stealing it
By receiving it as a gift
B.explanation: Kamala says love "can be obtained by begging, buying, receiving it as a gift, finding it in the street, but it cannot be stolen." Finding, buying and receiving are all on her list of ways that work, so only stealing cannot obtain it.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "penetrated" most nearly means
options: admired greatly
seen through
avoided
painted
B.explanation: The world was a veil "destined to be penetrated and destroyed by thought," so to be penetrated is to be seen through. Admiring it is his new attitude, the opposite. "Painted" has no support. "Avoided" misses the idea of thought passing through the veil.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's thoughts about the people he meets suggest that he
options: thinks they are much wiser than the Samanas and Brahmins
regards them as kind but somewhat simple
fears them and avoids them
wants them as his new teachers
B.explanation: He calls them "thankful," "submissive," and says they "think little. Like children are all people," kind but simple. He does not rank them above Samanas. He smiles, so he does not fear them. He sees them as children, not teachers.

B.prompt: What does Siddhartha claim about magic?
options: It is simply the power of thinking, waiting and fasting, which anyone can use.
It is the work of daemons that only the oldest Samanas command.
It is a rare gift that only Kamala, of all people, is able to give him.
It cannot be learned by anyone at all.
B.explanation: He says "there are no daemons" and "Everyone can perform magic... if he is able to think... wait... fast." The daemon view is what "fools" believe. He learned it, so it can be learned. He credits the Samanas, not Kamala.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Siddhartha does nothing, he waits, he thinks, he fasts"
"This is what Siddhartha has learned among the Samanas."
"When you throw a rock into the water, it will speed on the fastest course"
"Everyone can perform magic, everyone can reach his goals, if he is able to think"
B.explanation: Only "Everyone can perform magic... if he is able to think" makes his claim about magic. The rock line is a comparison for how he moves, not a claim about magic. "He waits, he thinks, he fasts" lists his habits. "Learned among the Samanas" names where, not what magic is.

B.prompt: The sequence of actions with the barber's assistant mainly serves to
options: show Siddhartha shedding his Samana appearance step by step
show that Siddhartha now plans to become a barber in the city himself
show the city's customs for welcoming travellers
describe the temple of Vishnu in the city
B.explanation: Shaving the beard, cutting and oiling the hair, then bathing show him shedding the Samana look in steps. He does not plan to be a barber. The temple is only where he found the assistant. The actions serve his goal, not a description of city customs.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Kamala admires Siddhartha's torn loincloth and dusty feet.
Kamala asks Siddhartha to teach her what the Samanas know.
Kamala laughs that a ragged Samana, unlike her rich visitors, wants to learn from her.
Kamala sends him away, since she never teaches anyone who comes to her from the forest.
B.explanation: She marvels that a Samana "with long hair and an old, torn loincloth" comes, unlike young men with "beautiful clothes" and "money." She does not refuse in this passage. She mocks rather than admires the loincloth. She does not ask him to teach her.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "admonished" most nearly means
options: fed
warned
dressed
praised
B.explanation: He was "urgently admonished to get himself out of the grove as soon as possible without being seen," so he was warned. Praise is wrong; the escape had not happened yet. "Dressed" and "fed" are other things done for him but do not fit the urgent instruction.

B.prompt: The short sentences "I can think. I can wait. I can fast." mainly serve to
options: present Siddhartha's skills plainly and confidently
show that Siddhartha is embarrassed to have so few skills
list the daily duties of a merchant
repeat Kamala's own words back to her
B.explanation: Three short, parallel claims present his skills plainly. He is not embarrassed; later he insists these skills are useful. They are a Samana's skills, not a merchant's duties. Kamala asked the question; the words are his answer, not a repetition of hers.

B.prompt: The ferryman's words suggest that he
options: is greedy and carries only paying travellers
dislikes the river and his work on it
distrusts Samanas and their ways
expects no payment from a poor guest
B.explanation: He says "I haven't expected any payment from you and no gift," adding "You will give me the gift another time," so he expects nothing from a poor guest. That rules out greed. He says of the river, "I love it more than anything," so he does not dislike it. He welcomes the Samana, so he does not distrust Samanas.

B.prompt: Kamala compares love with a Samana's learning mainly in order to
options: prove that Samanas know more about love than anyone else in the city
make fun of the Brahmins and their learning
change the subject away from money
show that what is truly one's own cannot be taken by force
B.explanation: She asks whether a Samana ever feared someone would "steal his learning," then says "precisely like this" with love, which cannot be stolen. She does not call Samanas her teachers. She does not mock Brahmins. The comparison answers his threat directly.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 respond to the doubt implied in Passage 1?
options: It changes the subject to Kamala's beauty and dress.
It shows Kamala agreeing with him immediately.
It argues that thinking, waiting and fasting are powerful skills.
It admits his skills are useless and that he needs a better trade.
B.explanation: Passage 1 has Kamala doubt that his skills are enough; in Passage 2 Siddhartha says anyone "able to think... wait... fast" can reach his goals. He does not admit uselessness. Her beauty is not the topic. Kamala is not shown agreeing in Passage 2.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha learned his magic from Kamala in the pleasure-garden.
Siddhartha reaches his goals by hard work and the help of daemons.
Siddhartha reaches goals by letting nothing in his soul oppose them.
Siddhartha has no goals at all in the city.
C.explanation: "His goal attracts him, because he doesn't let anything enter his soul which might oppose the goal." He "does nothing" and says "there are no daemons," so hard work and daemons are wrong. He has a goal. He learned this "among the Samanas," not from Kamala.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's earlier view of the world was
options: distrustful and dismissive
based on a love of travel
taught to him by the ferryman
joyful and childlike
C.explanation: In former times he "looked upon" the world "in distrust," as a veil to be destroyed, so his view was dismissive. Joy and delight describe his new view. Travel is not named. The ferryman appears later and is not the source.

C.prompt: The contrast between "in former times" and "But now" mainly serves to
options: mark the change in how Siddhartha sees the world
introduce the ferryman and his hut
compare his childhood with his years among the Samanas
show that nothing in him has changed
C.explanation: The structure sets his old distrust against his "liberated eyes" now, marking a change in vision. It compares two ways of seeing, not stages of his life such as childhood. It shows change, not sameness. The ferryman does not appear in this passage.

C.prompt: How does Siddhartha compare his new worldly goals with his life as a Samana?
options: He cannot tell the two kinds of goals apart.
The new goals seem small and easy; the old life was hard.
Both seem to him equally hopeless and empty.
The new goals seem far harder than anything he faced as a Samana.
C.explanation: He calls the Samana life "difficult, toilsome, and ultimately hopeless" and says now "everything is easy," with "small, near goals." That reverses the second choice. Only the old life is called hopeless, not both. He clearly separates the two lives, so he can tell them apart.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Everything was difficult, toilsome, and ultimately hopeless, when I was still a Samana."
"I need clothes and money, nothing else; this a small, near goals, they won't make a person lose any sleep."
"Now, everything is easy, easy like that lessons in kissing, which Kamala is giving me."
"Simple is the life which people lead in this world here," thought Siddhartha.
C.explanation: Only the "small, near goals" line names the new goals and their ease. "Simple is the life" describes others' life generally. The "everything is easy" line describes ease but names no goals. The "difficult, toilsome" line describes only the old life, half of the comparison.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "devotion" most nearly means
options: hobby
loyalty to a friend
piety
love affair
C.explanation: A Samana's "religious devotion" is listed with "his learning" and "his depth of thought," so it means piety. Loyalty to a friend misses "religious." "Love affair" is a different sense. "Hobby" trivializes something the passage treats as a Samana's very own and most serious possession.

C.prompt: The ferryman's statement that he has "looked into its eyes" suggests that he
options: has never truly studied the river
fears the river and its currents
has hurt his eyes from years of bright sun on water
treats the river almost as a living companion
C.explanation: Giving the river "eyes" treats it as a living being he knows, and he says he has "learned from it." Eye damage is not mentioned. He loves it "more than anything," so he does not fear it. He has often listened to it and learned from it, so he has studied it.

C.prompt: Kamala's words suggest that, in her world,
options: wealth and appearance matter a great deal
Samanas are frequent and welcome visitors
learning is valued above clothes and money
Brahmins are never welcome at all
C.explanation: Her visitors come "in beautiful clothes... fine shoes... money in their pouches," and she treats a ragged Samana as a joke, so appearance and wealth matter. Learning is not shown as more valued. She says this "never" happened before, so Samanas are rare. Sons of Brahmins do come.

C.prompt: The repetition of "All are" in Siddhartha's thoughts mainly serves to
options: show that he has met and knows every person in the land
show his friend Govinda's opinion of people
praise each person he meets by name
show him making a sweeping judgment about people
C.explanation: "All are thankful... All are submissive... Like children are all people" sweeps everyone into one judgment. He has met few people. No one is named. These are Siddhartha's own thoughts, not Govinda's opinion, though he says the people are like Govinda.

C.prompt: The detail of giving the rice cake to a dog mainly serves to
options: show how hungry he has become
show that the rice cake was spoiled
show that he has always loved animals more than people
show Siddhartha's pride in no longer being a beggar
C.explanation: The narrator links it to pride: "He was no Samana any more, it was no longer becoming to him to beg." No love of animals is stated. Nothing says the cake was spoiled. He "remained without food," so the act shows pride over hunger.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 relate to the ferryman's words in Passage 1?
options: Siddhartha decides to stay and learn from the river.
Siddhartha argues angrily with the ferryman.
Siddhartha underrates the wisdom the ferryman expresses.
Siddhartha pays the ferryman with money.
C.explanation: The ferryman says "much can be learned from a river," yet Siddhartha thinks all such people "think little," underrating him. He leaves, so he does not stay. He has no money. They part "smiling," without any argument, and Siddhartha is happy about the ferryman's kindness.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 follow from the realization in Passage 1?
options: He asks Kamala's servants for new clothes.
He acts on it by changing his appearance.
He ignores it and enters the grove just as he is.
He gives up his goal and returns to the forest.
C.explanation: In Passage 1 he sees he "must not remain like this"; in Passage 2 he has his beard shaved and hair oiled. He pursues "his goal," not the forest. He does not enter the grove as he is. The servants give garments later, not in Passage 2.
